title: Draft: extcap: control pipe
description:
Create shutdown pipe which allows to notify extcap about stopping a capture
to allow it to clean up.

Changes:
- staff for control pipes for toolbox communication was renamed to toolbox*,
  just CLI commands stays control*
- ciscodump adapted to use shutdown pipe
- user documentation updated
- developer documentation updated

notes.body: marked this merge request as **draft**

You cannot rename extcap arguments because it will break existing extcap plugins. And because of this you should not rename the internal names.

What about using one of the existing pipes for your purpose?
Dear Stig, I changed toolbar pipes back to original names. Are you able to verify your extcap with it?

Hi. Thank you for comments, I'm open to discussion. There are my reasons why I did it current way...

I spent several weeks with trying to use existing pipes to make it stopping extcap. But it mean to change complete design of toolbar pipes. The point is that:
1. Toolbar code is in ui/Qt and is not related to start/stop actions. It is destined to pass user related information.
2. Two pipes with many commands are complex to implement it for every extcap.
3. Stopping capability should be optional for extcap and simple oneway control path is enough. BTW I was "inspired" by relation between wireshark and dumpcap. I'm trying to unify code for stopping dumpcap and extcap where possible.

Current pipes are destined for toolbar, not for control. That is reason why they are processed in Qt part of code.
But in real, I found no public plugin which use toolbar pipes except python example in doc/. Do you know another?

That is reason why I renamed it. And I adapted all existing public plugins and examples/doc for it. So I don't think it broken something. But I might be wrong.

On the other hand I can revert renaming during work, but I think that current naming (at least in code) is more clear.

There is a lot of work on the change, I'm still working on Windows part...

The intention of the control pipes was to make them generic, but because of development time constraints the pipe handling code was added to UI/Qt. This should be refactored into extcap. It should not be needed to implement every command when using this pipes, but I don't remember all details to tell if the stopping capability easily can be added.

The extcap toolbar was first made for the [nRF Sniffer for Bluetooth LE](https://www.nordicsemi.com/Products/Development-tools/nRF-Sniffer-for-Bluetooth-LE), and I have also seen several in-house plugins using the extcap toolbar.

I'm sorry I really was not aware of any other extcaps using the API. BTW your code is C or python?

I'm afraid that refactoring to extcap will be very difficult, but lets discuss its goals:
- be able to support:
    - no pipe
    - unidirectional pipe from WS to extcap (I did it now)
    - two unidirectional pipes between WS and extcap
- be extendable (to support new commands in future)

My idea is to implement callbacks which wireshark code will register on one side and extcap code will register on its side. So anyone will be able to send/receive any commands. But it still mean that all extcaps must be adapted - it is one of reasons why I implemented another pipe just for unidirectional communication.

For extendability we must support something like capability check - to ensure that extcap and wireshark understand same set of commands. Without it we can't warn user that extcap do not match wireshark set...

I can try to develop "parallel" pipes to current one. So old code can use current schema and new/adapted extcaps can use new schema. But I'm not sure whether it is good approach.

Do you think that just renaming of CLI parameters back would be enough?

I don't like having one extra pipe with only one use case to send a "quit" message to the extcap process. We already have control pipes which could be used for this. The code for handling control pipes should be moved from UI (`interface_toolbar.cpp` and `interface_toolbar_reader.cpp`) to extcap, and a new control command (`commandControlShutdown`) added for this purpose. This will both improve existing functionality and add support for using the control pipes in `tshark`.

I don't like renaming internal names which is unrelated to the main purpose of this change. If applicable (which I don't think it is) this should be done in a separate MR.

I see. There are two topics. I will start from back.

I will move renaming to different MR, it makes sense.

The problem with moving shutdown command to current control pipes is different that just you mentioned.

None of current extcaps can be shutdown from wireshark. It is not so obvious on unix like systems (they use signals), but it is visible on Windows. My point of view is that we need that every/most extcap should support shutdown.

Lets imagine that it will be implemented with control pipes somehow. As consequence of it, UI will show toolbar dialog for every run extcap even it is simple as udpdump, ciscodump or randpkg. It looks weird to me and it is reason why I separated it from control pipes.

In other words, most of extcaps needs only shutdown part of control pipes.

Another point of view:

If we will modify control pipes to support shutdown, UI will show toolbar dialog. To avoid it, control pipes must be extended with some kind of capabilites - extcap should inform wireshark, whether it requires only shutdown or more functions. Based on it, UI would be able to show/do not show toolbox.

But this change will break everything in extcap API!

I propose to discuss it on core forum...

Sending SIGTERM is the way for Unix systems. While Wireshark currently does send SIGTERM to extcap, it does so only after the pipes have been closed and without really allowing any time for process to react.

The cross-platform solution would be to use `stdin`. But we just close `stdin` right away in `extcap_init_interfaces()`. If we decided to use `stdin` to signal quit, then extcaps would have to be made aware of it (and distinguish between old Wireshark version that just close `stdin` unconditionally right after starting Wireshark).

This is bad pattern and it should not longer be used. The whole reason for that was leaking handle. But hopefully the root cause has been [identified and fixed](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7436/diffs?commit_id=1323544f658f73334d8b26c945781552e5714d16).

The proper solution I believe is to use GIOStream and handle the asynchronous events using callback passed to `g_io_add_watch()`. It cannot be plugged in just yet due to semi-blocking structure (instead of truly asynchronous handling) that was possible by this ugly peek-into-pipe workaround.
I'm sorry, but I didn't get it. Is there any example use of it in wireshark? BTW does it work on windows?

The current use is in `packet-snort.c`, but that was written years ago before the GLib mainloop was handled properly. Using `GIOChannel` watch is pretty much similar to [g_unix_fd_add used recently](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7558/diffs?commit_id=df7f3e76b5cd1193cd22b399920e80b9faabfd24). Basically instead of `fd` in callback, you get `GIOChannel`. I didn't change it yet because it would require changing from `fd` to `GIOChannel` on quite many functions, and there still are more important low-level issues.

The whole point of that `GIOChannel` works on Windows. Otherwise plain `g_unix_fd_add()` would be fine. It seems that the only easy to use replacement to fd polling that works on Windows and other platforms is `GIOChannel`. While we could try to create our own solution, I don't think it is appropriate. We use GLib anyway and it is better to use some good proven code instead of rolling up your own (the danger with rolling up own code is that some issues can be covered up for years, like the [leaky pipes](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/7436/diffs?commit_id=1323544f658f73334d8b26c945781552e5714d16)).

I briefly read GIOChannel documentation and it looks that it works fine on Linux, but is limited on Windows. So I see no reason to change it.

Note about leaking handle:
I don't thin it is leaking handle in this case. The handle is created by an extcap, is used by same extcap/process and is closed by same process. The thread is started just for reason to be able to pool the handle independently on main thread.

> I briefly read GIOChannel documentation and it looks that it works fine on Linux, but is limited on Windows. So I see no reason to change it.

Windows support for GIOChannel is sufficient for Wireshark use case. Only one `#ifdef` is required (`g_io_channel_win32_new_fd()` on Windows, `g_io_channel_unix_new()` on UNIX), the rest of the code (that is after the fd is created) will be common.

> Note about leaking handle: I don't thin it is leaking handle in this case. The handle is created by an extcap, is used by same extcap/process and is closed by same process. The thread is started just for reason to be able to pool the handle independently on main thread.

It *was* leaking handle that led to this bad pattern. The peek-before-read is the only way to prevent deadlock on blocking read when the handle leaks. If the handle leaks, then `read()` call will never notice broken pipe, and as such will hang forever after the child process finishes. Solving the leak makes `read()` behave as expected, i.e. it does return with 0 bytes read when the child process closes the other end of pipe.

GIOChannel does exactly what is needed (allows polling the pipe descriptor) in a way that is transparent to the platform (it does create new thread under the hood to overcome Windows API limitations). Taking advantage of the struggle GLib developers went through is way better than coming up with custom solutions.

Semi-blocking behavior is really bad and leads to convoluted code. It does so in a way that disguises itself as simple solution. But in reality, this falsely perceived simplicity leads to so many issues that everyone who took their time to identify, trace and fix (in any sufficiently big project) seems to come to the same conclusion. That is, try to get a single event loop and make use of it. See #15743 for example.

To use `GIOChannel` watches something has to poll the event loop. This can be achieved with `g_main_loop_run()`, but really `g_main_context_iteration()` is enough. The code that operates on multiple events should really return to event loop as soon as possible instead of coming up with nasty workarounds (e.g. calling `QCoreApplication::processEvents()` or `g_main_context_iteration()` in arbitrary functions).

I think the control pipe is simply too complex solution to the problem you are trying to solve.

Yes, g_main_context_iteration() is enough, I missed it. But if the application is single threaded, I have to incorporate it to every internal loop etc.

Pipe handling just starts one additional thread which checks just pipe status. So application stays as it was (e.g. single threaded). So I see no advantage for GIOChannel and related stuff.

About shutdown pipe - yes, signals look more simple, but as we agreed in wireshark-dev, they are platform dependent and on Win32 it looks very complex to me. pipe is more straightforward and proven solution (dumpcap use it).

> About shutdown pipe - yes, signals look more simple, but as we agreed in wireshark-dev, they are platform dependent and on Win32 it looks very complex to me. pipe is more straightforward and proven solution (dumpcap use it).

I don't agree on the "we agreed in wireshark-dev" part. Also, regarding dumpcap there is a reason the `-Z` option is hidden! All comments clearly state that this is the workaround, not a solution. Having the workaround stay for years does not mean that it should spread as the proven solution.

As @gpotter2 says, I believe I implemented all of this taking @stigbjorlykke's concerns about backwards compatibility and using the existing pipe into account and moving the code into `extcap.c` and using GLib sources (since @desowin had previously made sure that the glib main loop is running.) I couldn't entirely use GIOChannel directly on Windows because the pipe is setup for overlapped reads on Windows, which still don't seem to play entirely nice with GIOChannel. (I'm not entirely certain that they need to be overlapped I/O when there's two separate pipes for each direction.)

It works well for me on Windows with all the extcaps that I've used. Right now (partially for testing) it will send the Quit message over the pipe on Linux as well (and fall back to using signals if it doesn't work.)

+==== Extcap greaceful shutdown
+
+Extcap code can be run by Wireshark or directly by command line/console. In both cases
+the code can require to make cleanup before it is terminated - make graceful shutdown.
+Shutdown is initiated by Wireshark and if the extcap do not exit in 30 seconds, it is
+terminated.
+
+For extcaps in C which requires graceful shutdown, there is `extcap/extcap-base.h`
+call `extcap_base_register_graceful_shutdown_cb()`. The call must be called to inform
+the framework that graceful shutdown is requested.
+
+Then, before extcap is terminated, global variable `extcap_end_application` is set
+to `TRUE`. Therefore application can check it e.g. in main loop whether it should exit.
+If callback is registered, it is called too.
+
+
+[source,c]
+----
+int main(int argc, char *argv[])
+{
+    ...
+
+    /* Graceful shutdown is requested */
+    if (!extcap_base_register_graceful_shutdown_cb(extcap_conf, NULL))
+        goto end;
+
+    /* Setup what should be cleaned up later, e.g. configure a device */
+    setup();
+
+    /* Main loop */
+    {
+        /* Read data from source */
+        read_data();
+
+        /* Write it to Wireshark */
+        libpcap_write_packet(...);
+
+        /* Loop till extcap_end_application is set by signal handler */
+    } while (!extcap_end_application);
+
+    /* Cleanup configuration */
+    cleanup();
+
+end:
+    ...
+}
+----
+
+==== Extcap graceful shutdown on Windows
+
+For Windows systems Wireshark implements shutdown pipe to be able to inform a extcap that shutdown
+is requested. Wireshark creates the queue, pass its name to the extcap and writes word `QUIT` to
+the pipe when shutdown is requested.
+
+Extcap should read the pipe and when command is received it should cleanup and quit. Wireshark waits
+30 s till the extcap is terminated as usually.
+
+To notify Wireshark that extcap is capable of shutdown pipe, it should exhibit `shutdown`
+keyword in configuration query.
+
+.Example of interface definition with shutdown pipeline
+[source,bash]
+----
+$ extcap_example.py --extcap-interfaces
+extcap {version=1.0}{display=Example extcap interface}
+interface {value=example1}{display=Example interface 1 for extcap}
+shutdown {value=shutdown}
+----
+
+When extcap is graceful shutdown capable, it will receive `--shutdown <pipe>` argument during
+start.
+
+As mentioned above, for extcaps in C `extcap/extcap-base.h` contains
+`extcap_base_register_graceful_shutdown_cb()` call to notify framework that it is shutdown pipe
+capable. When the call is used, framework starts thread which monitors the pipe and sets global
+variable `extcap_end_application` to `TRUE` when `QUIT` is sent from Wireshark.
+
+[source,c]
+----
+int main(int argc, char *argv[])
+{
+    char* help_url;
+    extcap_parameters * extcap_conf = g_new0(extcap_parameters, 1);
+
+    /* Init extcap_base configuration */
+    help_url = data_file_url("example.html");
+    extcap_base_set_util_info(extcap_conf, argv[0], CISCODUMP_VERSION_MAJOR, CISCODUMP_VERSION_MINOR,
+      CISCODUMP_VERSION_RELEASE, help_url);
+
+    /* extcap supports shutdown pipe */
+    extcap_base_register_graceful_shutdown_cb(extcap_conf, NULL);
+
+    while ((result = ws_getopt_long(argc, argv, ":", longopts, &option_idx)) != -1) {
+
+        switch (result) {
+        case OPT_...:
+            ...
+        default:
+            /* Process any extcap_base parameter including shutdown pipe */
+            if (!extcap_base_parse_options(extcap_conf, result - EXTCAP_OPT_LIST_INTERFACES, ws_optarg)) {
+                  ws_warning("Invalid option: %s", argv[ws_optind - 1]);
+                  goto end;
+            }
+        }
+    }
+
+    /* Setup what should be cleaned up later, e.g. configure a device */
+    setup();
+
+    /* Main loop */
+    {
+        /* Read data from source */
+        read_data();
+
+        /* Write it to Wireshark */
+        libpcap_write_packet(...);
+
+        /* Loop till extcap_end_application is set by signal handler */
+    } while (!extcap_end_application);
+
+    /* Cleanup configuration */
+    cleanup();
+
+end:
+    ...
+}
+----
